question:
Three flower beds overlap as shown. Bed \(A\) has \(500\) plants, bed \(B\) has \(450\) plants, and bed \(C\) has \(350\) plants. Beds \(A\) and \(B\) share \(50\) plants, while beds \(A\) and \(C\) share \(100.\) The total number of plants is

[Figure 1](figures/1999_AMC_8_Q09_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The diagram shows that beds \(B\) and \(C\) do not overlap. We can therefore count bed \(A\) first, then add only the new plants from each other bed.

Count all \(500\) plants in \(A\). Of the \(450\) plants in \(B\), the \(50\) shared with \(A\) have already been counted, leaving \(450-50=400\) new plants. Similarly, \(C\) contributes \(350-100=250\) new plants. None of these new plants from \(C\) belongs to \(B\), because those two beds do not overlap.

These groups include every plant exactly once, so the total is
\[
500+400+250=1150.
\]
There are \(\boxed{1150}\) plants, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

edges.reason: Column addition reinforces place-value alignment and regrouping. Mental hundreds/tens sums can be obtained by decomposition and unit counts without laying out written columns.
Mental arithmetic on hundreds and tens uses the values of those places in three-digit numbers.
Column subtraction provides regrouping experience. Decomposition, counting-on or subtraction of unit counts can compute the oral result without that written algorithm.
Mental addition prepares unit-count decomposition and inverse checks. Subtracting hundreds/tens can be performed directly on the corresponding counts without an earlier mental-addition routine.

Written subtraction supports removing a duplicated overlap when counts are larger. Counting disjoint regions or using decomposed mental subtraction avoids the column algorithm without changing the overlap reasoning.
edges.scope: computing totals while removing double-counted overlap
